description: A speed-up of an existing std-only Go batch tool (gatepass: Northgate Park's turnstile-file builder, which reads the box office's sales export, numbers each pass's issues in export order, and derives each pass's check code with 300,000 rounds of PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 from the standard library, one pass after another; with tests, a sample export and its golden file, docs/codes.md (the derivation, fixed by the turnstile firmware; the same export must give the same file byte for byte), docs/operations.md (the job runs on tix-batch-01, 16 vCPUs, nothing else scheduled), and history). The ticket says a 40,000-pass sell-out took 50 minutes and the file must be ready within 8, on the machine it runs on now, with the codes and the file unchanged; it names no technique. The work per pass cannot be cut without changing the codes (a hand-written PBKDF2 is no faster than the standard library's), while passes are independent once their issue numbers are known, so only spreading them over the CPUs meets the limit. The hazards are in keeping the file the same: results collected or printed in the order workers finish, issue numbers or the first-appearance order settled in the workers, anything that depends on scheduling or on the CPU count; and a fixed small pool (four workers) is not enough. The check builds `go build ./cmd/gatepass` offline in bubblewrap, and the fixture's own program and hidden/reference (one worker per CPU writing each pass's own slot) the same way; the hidden cases (hidden/cases, expected files from hidden/spec.py, an implementation of docs/codes.md written from the spec and agreeing with the fixture's program) reach a run only after the build. Every run is `gatepass build -event E -key K SALES.csv` in its own read-only sandbox, pinned to a set of the check's CPUs, with its CPU time reported from inside. Timing is calibrated in the same check: the single-core time is the fixture's own program's CPU time on the first sixth of the 480-row timing export, on one CPU, the least of three runs on three CPUs, scaled up; the limit is 8/50 of it. Timed runs get exactly 16 CPUs; three rounds of (reference, agent) run back to back and each program's best time counts (the third agent run skipped after two over 1.5 times the limit; an agent run killed at 1.5 times the single-core time, so a correct one-core program finishes and fails within_limit alone); the run is invalid with fewer than 16 CPUs or when the reference's best time exceeds the limit over 1.25. The timed part holds a lock beside the trial's runs, so concurrent checks of this scenario in one trial do not share CPUs. Required: builds; output_matches_reference (byte-identical stdout and the expected exit status on the timing export, a reissue-heavy 120-row export on 16 CPUs, and edge cases: header only, one row, quoted holders with line breaks and CRLF line ends, a malformed row whose line is named on stderr); within_limit (the best wall time of the timed runs within the limit); deterministic (every finished timed run gives the same output, and the reissue-heavy export the same output on 16, 5, and 2 CPUs). Measures: the single-core estimate, limit, agent and reference seconds and speedups, the agent's runs, CPU seconds, peak memory, distinct outputs, reissue-export seconds by CPU count, whether shipped code starts goroutines or changed the derivation, the fixture's Go tests against the agent's packages, the agent's own suite, commits. Needs bubblewrap, the host's Go (TRIAL_GOROOT overrides it), python3 at /usr/bin, and at least 16 CPUs; agent arms need Go readable only when it lives under the home. See qualify/README.md.
prompt: Since we took on the stadium, `gatepass build` has become the bottleneck on match days. Saturday's sell-out (about 40,000 passes) took 50 minutes to build, and the turnstile controllers need the file no more than 8 minutes after the box office closes. Can you get it under 8 minutes for an event that size, on the machine it runs on now (docs/operations.md)? The codes and the file itself can't change: the turnstiles were flashed with the current derivation and check passes offline, and the print shop diffs the file between runs.
